idiom_name: Record<Message["kind"], Handler> registry validated with satisfies, swapped at runtime
implementation_notes: TypeScript's contribution is compile-time checking of a runtime rule base: model the message as a discriminated union, keep destinations in a Record keyed by the union's discriminant values, and attach satisfies Record<Message["kind"], Handler> so a missing destination is a type error while the object keeps its precise literal type. Runtime swaps then replace the whole record and consumers narrow the message with a switch on the discriminant (a never-typed default proves exhaustiveness). The satisfies check and narrowing happen at compile time while the swap stays a runtime operation, which is exactly the split the pattern needs; keep an exhaustive switch instead when the rules must not change without a build.
pitfalls: satisfies checks the literal you write: once a rule set arrives as JSON and is assigned to the record type, nothing is validated - parse it through a runtime schema before assigning.
An index signature such as Record<string, Handler> makes every lookup possibly undefined unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is on; keep the key union closed and provide an explicit default.
Handlers that read a module-level registry see the newest value at call time, so one message can be routed by two rule generations; snapshot the record per message when that matters.
